newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST - DB seen matching yr-ago H1 profit.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - DB seen matching yr-ago H1 profit.

text.p: New Zealand brewer DB Group Ltd is expected this week to report flat first half earnings of around NZ$15-16 million, analysts said on Monday.
DB reported a net profit of NZ$16.0 million in the six months to March, 1996, and declining overall beer consumption is expected to constrain profits this time around in the figures due on Wednesday.
One analyst, who expected a net profit of NZ$16.6 million, said a key element would be to what extent DB's packaging division comes to its aid.
Likewise, an expected increase in sales of Dutch lager Heineken, brewed here under licence, may go some way to offset declines in consumption of some local brews.

Over the full year to September, the company is set to go from being a net interest earner to being a net payer of interest after its capital restructure in May. Analysts currently expect an annual profit of around NZ$24 million.

"There is a heavy seasonal influence there but certainly it is complicated by the fact that for the first six months there is a reasonably sizeable interest-received column and in the second half there will be an interest expense," analyst John Cairns at Cavill White Securities said.
Heineken, while a small part of the market, was nevertheless likely to put in a strong showing, especially with the company now expanding production ahead of schedule.
"The beer market has become increasingly fragmented and Heineken is in a niche that is actually growing, whereas the overall market is declining," Cairns said.
"It's a product they would get very healthy markups from and in terms of the perception of the group it adds that much more credibility to its presence," Cairns added.
DB is majority owned by Asia Pacific Breweries Ltd, a joint venture between Heineken NV and Frazer and Neave Ltd.

In April, DB's main competitor, Lion Nathan, reported a 21 percent slump in the first half profit to NZ$72.2 million. Lion blamed competitive markets in New Zealand and Australia for the decline, plus a slightly higher tax rate.
